meta.title: Timetabling software for schools and universities
meta.description: Calendry places a whole term in about 350 milliseconds and hands you the proposal to judge. Rooms, cohorts, staff and courses in one place, for schools and universities.

hero.lead: Calendry holds every room, cohort, lecturer and course your term is made of, then proposes placements for all of it in about 350 milliseconds. Nothing reaches the live schedule until somebody applies it.
hero.titleLineTwo: A person still signs it off.
hero.proof: The code is public. Every capability on this page is covered by this repository's integration suite.

audience.line: For the people who actually build the timetable: registrars, timetabling officers and department heads, plus the lecturers who have to live in the result.

built.title: What works today
built.lead: Not a demo reel. Everything below is implemented, in use against a real database, and covered by this repository's integration suite.

next.title: Not built yet, and honest about it
next.lead: Calendry is being built in phases, and each of these is a phase rather than a promise with a date on it. Where a decision is still open, it says which one.

why.title: Decisions worth defending
why.lead: Timetabling software fails in specific, recognisable ways. These are the choices made against them. Each one is a rule the codebase is actually built on, not a slogan.

contact.title: Tell us about your institution
contact.lead: Calendry is being built for real timetables, so the useful conversation is about yours: how many rooms and cohorts, what your week looks like, and what breaks today.

problem.title: A term is a hundred constraints in a spreadsheet nobody dares open
problem.lead: Timetabling software fails in specific, recognisable ways, and so does having none. Both failures have the same shape: the schedule knows less than the person holding it.

benefits.title: What you get
benefits.lead: Five things this does for the person who owns the week. Each one is a capability that exists today, not a direction of travel.

how.title: How it works
how.lead: Three steps, and the third one is yours.

faq.title: Questions we get asked
faq.lead: The first two are the ones that lose the sale. They are answered with a partial no and a no.

finalCta.title: Bring us your hardest week
finalCta.lead: The useful conversation is about your institution: how many rooms and cohorts, what your week actually looks like, and what breaks today.

schedule.title: Schedule view and editor
schedule.note: Week grid on a desktop, day agenda on a phone. Move, swap and lock, with clashes recorded rather than refused, and every edit appended to a log with an actor. A locked session’s lecturer can be overridden by hand, permanently.

manage.title: Management screens for the core entities
manage.note: Rooms, groups, people, courses, terms, the daily block grid and its breaks, plus a Ctrl+K palette that jumps to any of them. A course can state that one session needs several rooms at once, for a cohort too large for any single hall, and the scheduler places the combination. A class can be assembled from other classes, for a track two cohorts take together. A course can be restricted to particular rooms, or required to run online, and the two are combined rather than one quietly overruling the other.

calendar.title: Academic calendar periods
calendar.note: Holidays, breaks and exam weeks, with a preview of exactly which weeks change classification before you save. Two dates do not obviously imply four exam weeks, and sometimes they do.

events.title: Single events alongside recurring courses
events.note: Create a session that belongs to no course, such as an open day or a guest lecture, with its own room, groups and people.

icalExport.title: Download your schedule as a calendar file
icalExport.note: An .ics of your own sessions for a term, opened in whatever calendar app you already use. Real UTC times, converted from the institution’s own clock rather than sent as its own local clock hours.

personSearch.title: Finding a person by name
personSearch.note: Assigning people searches the institution as you type rather than listing it. The people already assigned stay on screen while you look for the next one.

exams.title: A lecturer asks for an exam; staff decide
exams.note: Request an exam on a module you lead, and see where the request got to. It reaches no timetable until somebody approves it, because an exam is a room and an hour the schedule has to find.

availability.title: Availability the lecturer enters
availability.note: A lecturer declares when they cannot teach, and which days, times and kinds of room they would rather have; staff approve or reject each declaration. Reaching only your own data is the point of that section.

solverIntegration.title: Solver integration, end to end
solverIntegration.note: Start a run, keep the result even if the solver restarts, review the proposal against the current schedule, then apply or discard it. A run that succeeds with rules still broken is still offered, with the breaches listed, rather than thrown away. A clash made by hand can be repaired without rebuilding the term: the repair moves as little as it can, and still produces a proposal to review.

constraints.title: Rules each institution configures for itself
constraints.note: Thirty rule types, switched on and weighted per institution: double booking, session counts, unavailability, online share, room rank and exam periods, plus the shape of a day: idle gaps, teaching without a break, how long it runs, and whether it crosses buildings. Rooms can be reserved across the institution, sized to the group actually attending, and kept consistent for a class across the week.

federation.title: Shared rooms across a federation
federation.note: Institutions in a consortium can share a lecture hall and see each other's occupancy of it, without seeing each other's schedules.

determinism.title: Reproducible runs
determinism.note: The same inputs and the same seed produce a timetable identical byte for byte, as long as the run ended on its move budget rather than on a clock, which the run itself reports.

auth.title: Signing in, and permission roles per institution
auth.note: One account can act in several institutions and picks which one when signing in. Roles are composed from a fixed catalogue of permissions, per institution, in the UI.

tenancy.title: A data model and API built for many institutions
tenancy.note: Institutions are isolated in the database itself, not only in application code. A query issued without institution context returns nothing rather than everything.

import.title: Import from CSV and Excel
import.note: For institutions arriving with years of spreadsheets. Whether the column mapping is guided or a fixed template is not decided yet.

export.title: A live calendar subscription, not just a download
export.note: The single .ics download is built. A stable URL your calendar app polls on its own is a different, harder question. A feed link is itself a credential, and it needs the same answer as letting a student view a schedule with no account.

notifications.title: Notification delivery
notifications.note: Calendry already works out who an edit affects. Nothing sends anything yet, so the answer currently goes to a screen instead of an inbox.

eventEdit.title: Editing a single event after creating it
eventEdit.note: Its time can be moved, but its room, groups and people cannot be changed. Correcting a mistake means deleting and recreating it.

candidates.title: Several candidate schedules to choose between
candidates.note: Needs a design pass before it needs code: candidates that differ only trivially would be worse than one result. It may not be built at all.

i18n.title: A translated interface
i18n.note: Under way now, German first, on the mechanism that made it safe to start: the locale is resolved once on the server and the interface is extracted a section at a time, so no page is ever half translated in the browser.

warn.title: Warn, never block
warn.body: A person editing a timetable usually knows something the rules do not. So an edit that breaks a hard rule is permitted, and the breach becomes queryable state attached to the schedule. Findable next week, not a toast you dismissed.

groups.title: Nested groups really do clash
groups.body: Booking a programme blocks its cohorts, and booking a cohort blocks the programme. Clash detection walks the whole ancestor and descendant relationship through a maintained closure, rather than comparing the two names it was handed.

isolation.title: Isolation in the database, not in the code
isolation.body: Every institution scoped table is guarded by row level security, and the application connects as a role that owns nothing. The failure mode of a mistake is seeing no rows, which is loud, rather than seeing someone else's, which is not.

time.title: Nothing about time is hardcoded
time.body: Days per week, blocks per day, block length and the uneven breaks between blocks come from each institution's own grid. There is no assumed Monday to Friday and no fallback shape anywhere. An institution without a grid gets an empty state, not a guess.

events.title: Every edit is an event
events.body: Creates, moves, swaps, deletes and locks are appended to a log, on top of the generation they started from, with the person who did it. Reading that history back has no screen yet. The log is being kept properly before there is anything to show it in.

techLead.note: That is a synthetic instance the size of a large university. The development database's own term runs all the way to convergence in about four seconds. Both numbers came off a benchmark rather than a pitch deck, and both will move as the constraint set grows.

app.title: The application
app.body: Nuxt and TypeScript over PostgreSQL. Tenant isolation is enforced by row level security policies; the schedule's history is an append only event log applied on top of a versioned snapshot.

solver.title: The solver
solver.body: A separate stateless Rust service, reached over gRPC against a shared schema. Hybrid constructive placement followed by large neighbourhood local search with simulated annealing, over thirty constraint types. It holds no database: every run is a complete snapshot the application sends it.

contact.messageLabel: What would you like to know?
contact.messagePlaceholder: How many rooms, how many cohorts, what you use today…
contact.opened: A draft should have opened in your email app, addressed to {email}. If nothing happened, your browser has no mail app configured. Write to us directly instead.
contact.asideTitle: Why this is an email and not a form
contact.asideBody: There is no sign up you can do yourself, and Calendry cannot send mail yet: notification delivery is on the list above, not behind us. A form that showed you a tick and filed your message nowhere would be worse than saying so, so this button composes a message in your own email app and you send it from your own account.
contact.asideContact: Or write to {link}. Accounts for an existing institution are created by its administrator.

error.name: Tell us who you are, so a reply has somewhere to go.
error.institution: Which school or university are you asking about?
error.messageTooLong: Keep this under {max} characters. The rest can go in the email itself.

footer.note: Multi tenant timetabling for schools and universities. Built in the open, one verified phase at a time.

calculator.adminSeatsHint: Only people who edit, lock or run the solver

before.title: What breaks today
before.body: The term lives in a file one person can safely edit. A double booked room is found by the lecturer who walks into it. A cohort's clash is invisible because the cohort is spread over four tabs, and moving one session means checking the other ninety by hand.

after.title: What changes
after.body: The term lives in one model that already knows a programme and its cohorts are the same people. A clash is recorded the moment you create it and is still findable next week. Move one session and you are told what it broke; ask for the whole week back and it returns in about four seconds.

tagline.lineOne: A timetable is a hundred small judgements.
tagline.lineTwo: Calendry makes the easy ninety and hands you the ten that matter.

solver.title: A term placed while you wait
solver.body: 27,000 sessions in about 350 milliseconds on a synthetic large university instance; the development term runs to convergence in about four seconds. What comes back is a proposal drawn against the schedule you already have, listing what it would change and what it could not satisfy. Nothing is applied until you apply it.

editing.title: An edit that breaks a rule is still allowed
editing.body: Move a session, swap two, or lock one so nothing may touch it. If the change clashes with something, Calendry lets you make it and records the breach as state you can look up afterwards. A person editing a timetable usually knows something the rules do not, so it does not block you, and it does not forget.

model.title: Your vocabulary stays yours
model.body: Role names, session types and room equipment are things you define, not a fixed list you translate into. Days per week, blocks per day, block length and the uneven breaks between them come from your own grid. There is no assumed Monday to Friday and no fallback week shape anywhere.

people.title: Everyone sees their own slice
people.body: You compose the permission roles for your institution, so who may read the schedule, who may move a session and who may run the solver are separate questions. Lecturers declare when they cannot teach and which days they would rather have; staff approve or reject each declaration.

isolation.title: One institution cannot read another
isolation.body: Isolation is enforced by row level security in Postgres itself, and the application connects as a database role that owns nothing. The failure mode of a mistake is seeing no rows, which is loud, rather than seeing someone else's, which is not.

describe.title: Describe your institution once
describe.body: Rooms, cohorts, staff, courses, terms and your own daily block structure, plus which of thirty rule types you want enforced and how much each one matters.

ask.title: Ask for a timetable
ask.body: Start a run, watch it work, and cancel it if you change your mind. The same inputs and the same seed return the same timetable, and the run itself reports whether it ended on its move budget or on the clock.

judge.title: Judge the proposal
judge.body: Read what it would change and what it could not satisfy, then apply it or throw it away. Every edit afterwards is appended to a log with the person who made it.

proof.repoTitle: You can read all of it
proof.repoBody: The application, the solver and the shared schema are public at {link}. There is no licence on the repository yet, so you may read the code without being free to reuse it, and which licence to use is a decision still to be made.

runTerm.q: Can Calendry run our term today?
runTerm.a: Partly, and the honest answer is a list rather than a yes. The schedule editor, the management screens, the solver end to end, the academic calendar, permission roles and institution isolation are built and covered by tests. Importing your existing spreadsheets is not, and nothing sends email yet. If your week has to arrive from a file this term, that is the gap to talk about first.

import.q: Can we import our existing spreadsheets?
import.a: Not yet, and it is the first thing a new institution needs. The reason it is not built is that the design is undecided: whether the column mapping is guided or a fixed template changes what the import is able to accept, and getting that wrong is worse than waiting. Until it exists, an institution's data is entered through the management screens.

decides.q: Does the solver decide our timetable for us?
decides.a: No. It returns a proposal shown against the schedule you already have, and nothing reaches the live timetable until a person applies it. A run that finishes with rules still broken is still offered to you, with the breaches listed, rather than thrown away as a failure.

breaks.q: What happens if a proposal breaks one of our rules?
breaks.a: You are warned, never blocked. The breach becomes queryable state attached to the schedule, so it is findable next week rather than a message somebody dismissed. That applies to your own edits as much as to the solver's.

week.q: Does it assume a Monday to Friday week and fixed period lengths?
week.a: No, and this is the one we would rather not be asked, because most timetabling tools do. Days per week, blocks per day, block length and the uneven breaks between blocks all come from your institution's own grid. There is no fallback shape anywhere: an institution without a grid gets an empty state rather than a guess.

federation.q: Can two institutions share a lecture hall without seeing each other's schedules?
federation.a: Yes. Institutions in a consortium can share a room and see each other's occupancy of it, and nothing else. The shared resource is owned by the federation rather than by either institution, and read access widens to exactly that.

permissions.a: You decide, per institution. Roles are composed in the interface from a fixed catalogue of permissions, so reading the schedule, moving a session and running the solver are separate grants. A lecturer reaches their own sessions and their own declarations and nothing else. One account can act in several institutions and picks which at sign in.

reproducible.q: Will the same request produce the same timetable twice?
reproducible.a: Yes, as long as the run ended on its move budget rather than on the clock, and the run reports which of the two it was. Given the same inputs and the same seed the result is byte identical. A run that stopped because it hit a time limit is not a comparable measurement, and Calendry will not present it as one.

cost.a: The base tier follows your student count, lecturers are charged by teaching load with a multiplier for how complex your week is, and admin seats are counted separately for the few people who actually edit. Students are never billed. The pricing page has the rates and a calculator you can put your own numbers into.

accounts.a: There is no self service sign up. An institution's administrator creates its accounts, which is why the action on this page is a conversation rather than a form. One account can belong to several institutions and chooses which one it is acting in when it signs in.

code.q: Can we read the code before we commit to anything?
code.a: Yes. The application, the solver and the schema they share are public repositories. There is no licence on them yet, so you may read the code but not yet reuse it, and choosing a licence is on the list of decisions still open.

risk.line: No sign up, nothing to install, and no obligation. A walkthrough is half an hour on a call, and it opens with what Calendry cannot do yet.
